Treatment regimens CsA as first-line therapy CsA was administered orally at an initial dose of 3 to 5 mg/kg/day. The dosage was adjusted based on therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) to maintain a target whole-blood trough concentration of 150 to 200 ng/mL. For patients transferred from other centers who were already receiving ongoing CsA therapy with suboptimal responses, CsA was continued and optimized strictly under TDM at our center. Patients were definitively classified as CsA-refractory and transitioned to sirolimus only after failing to respond to an optimized, TDM-guided CsA regimen. Sirolimus as salvage therapy For patients who transitioned to sirolimus due to CsA failure or intolerance, treatment was typically initiated at 2 mg/day, followed by a maintenance dose of 1 to 3 mg/day. Sirolimus as salvage therapy For patients who transitioned to sirolimus due to CsA failure or intolerance, treatment was typically initiated at 2 mg/day, followed by a maintenance dose of 1 to 3 mg/day. The dosage was adjusted to maintain a target whole-blood trough concentration of 2 to 4 ng/mL. Maintenance and tapering regimens For patients who achieved a stable CR or PR, the effective therapeutic dosage of CsA or sirolimus was typically maintained for at least 6 months. Following this maintenance phase, a slow and individualized tapering process was initiated if the disease remained stable. The tapering period typically spanned 1 to 2 years. Depending on individual disease stability and drug tolerance, some patients required indefinite treatment with a minimal maintenance dose to sustain hematologic remission. Response criteria and efficacy assessment Treatment response was evaluated according to the Chinese Expert Consensus (2020) criteria. To accurately assess treatment efficacy and exclude the transient effects of exogenous blood, hematological response was evaluated at least 4 weeks after the last red blood cell (RBC) transfusion. Complete remission (CR) was defined as normalization of hemoglobin levels (males >120 g/L, females >110 g/L), accompanied by normal white blood cell (WBC) and platelet counts. Partial remission (PR) was defined as a hemoglobin increase of >30 g/L from baseline or achievement of transfusion independence, accompanied by normal WBC and platelet counts. No response (NR) was defined as failure to meet the criteria for PR. The primary

remission (PR) was defined as a hemoglobin increase of >30 g/L from baseline or achievement of transfusion independence, accompanied by normal WBC and platelet counts. No response (NR) was defined as failure to meet the criteria for PR. The primary efficacy endpoint was the overall response rate (ORR). Secondary endpoints included the prevalence of STAT3/5b mutations, time to response (TTR), and DOR. Safety assessments focused on drug-specific adverse events, particularly CsA-induced nephrotoxicity and hypertension, as well as sirolimus-associated hyperlipidemia and mucositis. TTR was defined as the interval from the initiation of the respective immunosuppressive therapy (CsA or sirolimus) to the first documentation of CR or PR. For patients who did not achieve hematologic improvement or discontinued treatment due to lack of efficacy, TTR was recorded as NR in the final analysis. For patients who achieved a confirmed hematologic response but had irregular follow-up intervals resulting in delayed documentation, the exact TTR could not be accurately determined. These patients were included in the ORR analysis but excluded from the calculation of median TTR to minimize statistical bias. Mutational analysis Genetic mutation profiles were retrospectively collected from patients’ historical next-generation sequencing (NGS) reports, based on either hematological targeted panels (e.g., the MDS/AA 85-gene and 63+49-gene panels) or whole-exome sequencing (WES). Patients whose NGS panels did not explicitly cover STAT3 and STAT5b were classified as untested and excluded from the mutational analysis. Patients whose NGS panels did not explicitly cover STAT3 and STAT5b were classified as untested and excluded from the mutational analysis. For patients evaluated with WES or panels incorporating these specific targets, the STAT3/5b status was defined as wild-type in the absence of detectable variants, and as mutated if corresponding variants were identified. Statistical analysis Data were analyzed using SPSS Statistics 27.0. Normally distributed continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation, whereas non-normally distributed variables are presented as median (range). Normality was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Between-group comparisons were performed using the independent samples t-test for normally distributed data, the Mann-Whitney U test for non-normally distributed data, and the chi-square test for categorical variables. All statistical tests were two-sided, and a P- value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. For variables with missing values, cases were excluded only from the specific analyses involving those variables, and no data imputation was performed. For patients who achieved a stable therapeutic response, the daily dosage of CsA or sirolimus was gradually tapered in an individualized manner. This de-escalation was guided by TDM. The goal was to reach the minimum daily maintenance dose required to sustain the target whole-blood trough concentrations (150 to 200 ng/mL for CsA and 2 to 4 ng/mL for sirolimus) while minimizing drug-related toxicity. During the tapering phase, minor hematological fluctuations were promptly managed by temporary dose re-escalation. Because these fluctuations were successfully rescued by routine dose adjustments without requiring a change in the line of therapy, they were not classified as definitive clinical relapses. This proactive TDM-guided management, combined with the relatively short median follow-up period, explains the absence of documented relapses in this cohort. This retrospective cohort study primarily evaluated the efficacy of sirolimus as a salvage therapy for acquired PRCA, while also assessing the outcomes of standard first-line CsA treatment in a real-world tertiary care setting. The most notable finding is that sirolimus achieved an ORR of 54.5% in patients who were refractory or intolerant to CsA. This efficacy was particularly evident in patients with PRCA secondary to T-LGLL. Furthermore, exploratory genetic analysis suggested that although STAT3/5b mutations may be associated with poor responses to CsA, sirolimus retained therapeutic activity in this mutation-positive subgroup. The overall ORR for first-line CsA in this study was 25.0%, which is lower than the 60 to 80% reported in previous studies. 5 We propose two main clinical factors to explain this discrepancy. First, this difference is heavily attributable to referral bias. As the data were derived from a tertiary referral center, the cohort included a substantial proportion of patients transferred from other institutions. Many of these patients were admitted with ongoing but suboptimally managed CsA therapy from local hospitals. These patients inherently had a worse prognosis and a higher likelihood of ultimate CsA failure compared with newly diagnosed, treatment-naive patients. Second, we applied a strict intention-to-treat approach, classifying patients who discontinued CsA early due to drug intolerance as treatment failures. This conservative method yields a lower statistical ORR but provides a highly realistic reflection of real-world clinical challenges. This high refractory burden is particularly evident in the

This high refractory burden is particularly evident in the marked difference in CsA efficacy observed between primary PRCA (ORR 42.1%) and PRCA secondary to T-LGLL (ORR <10%). Although CsA remains a standard first-line treatment for T-LGLL, the poor outcomes observed in the secondary cohort highlight the clinical challenges associated with refractory T-LGLL, thereby underscoring the need for alternative therapeutic options. Previous studies have demonstrated the efficacy of sirolimus in refractory PRCA and T-LGLL. 10 , 20 , 21 The observed ORR of 54.5% in this pretreated population further supports the role of sirolimus as an effective second-line therapy. The difference in CsA efficacy between primary and secondary PRCA underscores the heterogeneity of PRCA pathogenesis. CsA exerts its immunosuppressive effects primarily through inhibition of calcineurin, thereby blocking the nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT) signaling pathway and suppressing interleukin-2 production. 22 This mechanism is particularly effective in primary autoimmune PRCA, in which T-cell dysregulation is typically mediated through conventional activation pathways. 1 , 8 , 20 The present findings are consistent with this mechanism, as response rates were significantly higher in primary PRCA than in secondary forms. In contrast, the poor response to CsA in secondary PRCA suggests the involvement of alternative pathogenic mechanisms that are not dependent on calcineurin signaling. Moreover, therapeutic success in secondary PRCA is often dependent on effective control of the underlying disease. Since CsA primarily acts as a symptomatic immunosuppressant, its inability to eliminate the primary pathogenic driver may limit its efficacy as monotherapy in this subgroup. The efficacy of sirolimus as a salvage therapy may be attributed to its distinct mechanism of action. As an mTOR inhibitor, sirolimus targets the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/protein kinase B/mTOR (PI3K/AKT/mTOR) signaling pathway, which plays a critical role in regulating cell proliferation and survival. 23 In secondary PRCA subtypes, particularly T-LGLL, constitutive activation of the STAT3 pathway is a recognized driver of clonal expansion. 13 , 24 , 25 Although mechanistic investigations were not conducted in this study, the observed trend, in which patients harboring STAT3/5b mutations were refractory to CsA but responsive to sirolimus, supports a plausible pharmacological hypothesis. Constitutive activation of STAT3/5b may reduce the dependence of pathogenic T cells on calcineurin signaling, thereby contributing to CsA resistance, whereas inhibition of the mTOR pathway may circumvent this mechanism. The response kinetics of sirolimus are consistent with its mechanism of action as an mTOR inhibitor, reflecting a gradual process of clonal suppression rather than immediate cytokine inhibition. Responders in the CsA group maintained continuous remission throughout the observation period. Similarly, patients in the sirolimus group achieved sustained disease control without documented relapse. This observation was particularly evident in patients with STAT3/5b mutations. Despite a relatively delayed onset of response, these patients maintained remission throughout follow-up. These findings suggest that, in patients with mutation-positive or refractory PRCA, sirolimus may serve not only as a bridging therapy but also as a definitive treatment capable of achieving long-term disease control. However, the precise biological role of STAT3/5b mutations remains to be fully elucidated. These observations should therefore be interpreted with caution and require validation in future mechanistic studies and larger clinical cohorts. 16 , 17 These findings support a stratified, precision medicine approach to the management of PRCA. Given the uniform CsA resistance observed in specific subgroups, our findings suggest that the clinical utility of sirolimus may extend beyond a strict second-line salvage role. First, as a single-center retrospective study, the findings are subject to selection bias. Specifically, many patients were transferred after suboptimal responses to unmonitored ongoing CsA therapy at local hospitals. These patients inherently carried a worse prognosis than newly diagnosed cases, which likely contributed to the relatively low overall response rate in our CsA cohort. Second, the sample size, especially within the genetic analysis subgroup, was limited, thereby reducing the statistical power to definitively establish the association between STAT3/5b mutations and treatment response. Third, due to the retrospective nature of this study and the frequent transfer of patients from primary hospitals, precise quantitative baseline bone marrow differential counts were unavailable for a subset of the cohort. Furthermore, outpatient follow-up intervals for blood tests were not strictly standardized. This irregular monitoring schedule introduces a potential analytical bias. It limits the highly precise evaluation of TTR and remains an inherent limitation of our real-world setting. Future directions Although CsA remains an effective first-line treatment for primary PRCA, the results highlight its limitations in cases associated with T-LGLL, particularly in refractory settings. Sirolimus demonstrates substantial efficacy as a salvage therapy in this population, addressing an important unmet clinical need. The differential treatment response according to STAT3/5b mutation status provides a rationale for incorporating genetic profiling into the diagnostic evaluation. The presence of these mutations is associated with a high likelihood of CsA resistance and a favorable long-term response to sirolimus, supporting their use in guiding patients toward targeted salvage therapy earlier in the disease course. Future prospective, multicenter studies with larger cohorts are required to validate these biomarker-driven therapeutic strategies.

Altogether, sirolimus demonstrates efficacy in both primary and secondary cases regardless of STAT3/5b status. While still exploratory, early genetic profiling may potentially facilitate the identification of patients who may not fully respond to CsA, warranting further validation for its use in guiding earlier transition to sirolimus salvage therapy.

Immunotherapy has revolutionized the treatment of multiple cancers. Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapies, which inhibit immunosuppressive receptors such as cytotoxic T-lymphocyte associated protein 4 and programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1)/programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), activate T cells and remodel the tumor immune microenvironment. 1 2 However, an immunosuppressive milieu remains a major barrier to effective immunotherapy in gastric cancer (GC). While the CheckMate 649 trial reported an objective response rate of 59% for combined ICB and chemotherapy, 3 anti-PD-1 monotherapy in the KEYNOTE-062 trial achieved only a 15.5% response rate, 4 highlighting the urgent need to identify novel regulators of the gastric tumor immune microenvironment and actionable therapeutic targets. Emerging evidence indicates that the gut microbiome not only contributes directly to tumor progression but also exerts systemic control over host immunity. 5 – 7 Specific microbial signatures have been linked to ICB efficacy across multiple malignancies. 8 – 11 Certain microbes promote cancer development via direct interactions with tumor cells, including Helicobacter pylori in GC, 12 13 Porphyromonas gingivalis in pancreatic cancer, 14 15 and Fusobacterium nucleatum in colorectal cancer. 16 17 Importantly, many gut microbes influence tumor progression primarily by modulating the tumor immune microenvironment. Preclinical studies and clinical trials have identified bacterial taxa associated with ICB responses, such as Bifidobacterium , Collinsella , Akkermansia muciniphila , and Parabacteroides , which enhance the activity of cytotoxic CD8 + T cells within the tumor microenvironment. 18 – 22 Given the

trials have identified bacterial taxa associated with ICB responses, such as Bifidobacterium , Collinsella , Akkermansia muciniphila , and Parabacteroides , which enhance the activity of cytotoxic CD8 + T cells within the tumor microenvironment. 18 – 22 Given the unique acidic environment of the stomach, the role of gastric-resident microbiota in shaping antitumor immunity remains largely unexplored. Streptococcus anginosus is a member of the S. anginosus group and is recognized as an opportunistic pathogen associated with a broad range of human diseases, including oral and periodontal infections, deep abscess formation, hepatobiliary infections, and bacteremia. Increasing evidence has linked S. anginosus to gastrointestinal malignancies, particularly esophageal squamous cell carcinoma and GC, where its enrichment correlates with chronic mucosal inflammation, epithelial injury, and tumor progression. In addition to its potential tumor-promoting effects, S. anginosus has been reported to induce pro-inflammatory cytokine production and remodel local immune responses, suggesting that it may contribute to cancer-associated inflammation and immune dysregulation. 23 – 26 However, whether S. anginosus directly shapes the gastric tumor immune microenvironment and influences the response to ICB remains unknown. Bacteria can regulate antitumor immunity through multiple mechanisms. They can present microbial antigens or mimic tumor-associated epitopes to activate antigen-specific CD8 + T cells, promoting recognition and elimination of cancer cells. 27 28 Additionally, microbial metabolites, including bile acids, short-chain fatty acids, branched-chain amino acids, and trimethylamine, can modulate natural killer and regulatory T-cell function, thereby influencing the tumor immune landscape.

Here, by integrating microbiome profiling in mouse models with validation in human gastric tumors, we demonstrate that S. anginosus functionally contributes to immunotherapy resistance rather than merely representing a tumor-enriched commensal. Mechanistically, S. anginosus promotes the accumulation of kynurenic acid (KA) within the tumor microenvironment, which suppresses CD8 + T-cell cytotoxicity and limits the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade. We further show that KA directly interacts with and induces integrin α2 (ITGA2), a collagen receptor integrin implicated in immune cell adhesion, migration, and intracellular signaling, in CD8 + T cells, leading to inhibition of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT)/mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling pathway and downstream regulation of lysosomal cathepsin V (CTSV), ultimately driving T-cell dysfunction. Importantly, genetic or pharmacologic targeting of ITGA2 restores CD8 + T-cell and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-CD8 + T cell cytotoxicity and synergizes with PD-1 blockade to enhance antitumor efficacy in vivo. Together, our findings establish a causal link between intratumoral bacteria, metabolite-mediated immune suppression, and therapeutic resistance, and identify a tractable microbiome-metabolite-integrin axis as a promising target for immunomodulatory intervention in GC.

ITGA2 silencing markedly restored IFN-γ and granzyme B expression in human CD8 + T cells ( figure 5 F), indicating that ITGA2 plays a causal role in KA-induced functional suppression. 18.2 + CD8 + T cells significantly enhanced their ability to induce apoptosis and lysis of GC cells in co-culture assays ( figure 5 G,H). Furthermore, when ITGA2-deficient CD8 + T cells were treated with KA, the suppressive effects of KA on IFN-γ and granzyme B production were largely abrogated ( figure 5 I), confirming that ITGA2 acts downstream of KA to mediate effector T-cell inhibition. To further investigate the interaction between KA and ITGA2, we performed Cellular Thermal Shift Assay (CETSA) together with a photoaffinity probe-based pull-down assay. CETSA demonstrated a reproducible increase in the thermal stability of ITGA2 following KA treatment across a range of temperatures compared with vehicle control, consistent with ligand-associated protein stabilization. Furthermore, the photoaffinity probe KP1 specifically enriched ITGA2 following ultraviolet (UV) crosslinking and streptavidin pull-down, whereas minimal ITGA2 signal was detected in the negative control probe KP2. Importantly, enrichment of ITGA2 by KP1 was markedly reduced in the presence of excess unlabeled KA, supporting the specificity of the interaction ( online supplemental figure 5 G,H). Collectively, these complementary biochemical approaches support a specific physical association between KA and ITGA2. Although accumulating evidence links gastrointestinal dysbiosis to GC, the role of intratumoral microbes in tumorigenesis and immune regulation remains poorly understood. In this study, through integrated microbiome, metabolomic, transcriptomic, and immunological analyses, we demonstrate that S. anginosus is consistently enriched within gastric tumor tissues and functions as a critical microbial driver of immunotherapeutic resistance. Functional studies across orthotopic, subcutaneous, and GF mono-colonization models further establish that S. anginosus accelerates tumor progression, suppresses CD8 + T-cell effector function, and attenuates the therapeutic efficacy of PD-1 blockade. These findings extend previous observations linking S. anginosus to gastric carcinogenesis by further supporting its role in shaping an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and limiting antitumor immunity. S. anginosus , a gram-positive bacterium commonly colonizing the oral cavity, has recently been identified as a gastric pathobiont capable of establishing persistent colonization in the murine stomach. It induces acute inflammatory responses characterized by robust upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines, followed by chronic gastritis associated with parietal cell atrophy, mucinous metaplasia, and epithelial dysplasia hallmarks of gastric precancerous lesions. 38 – 40 Moreover, S. anginosus infection reshapes the gastric microbiota, leading to the enrichment of pathogenic oral commensals such as Prevotella and Aggregatibacter , along with the depletion of beneficial B. pseudolongum . 41 Fu and colleagues have reported that S. anginosus promotes gastric tumorigenesis through direct interaction with gastric epithelial cells via the TMPC-ANXA2-MAPK signaling axis. 25 Consistent with this, we confirmed the protumorigenic potential of S. anginosus

beneficial B. pseudolongum . 41 Fu and colleagues have reported that S. anginosus promotes gastric tumorigenesis through direct interaction with gastric epithelial cells via the TMPC-ANXA2-MAPK signaling axis. 25 Consistent with this, we confirmed the protumorigenic potential of S. anginosus using both orthotopic GC mouse models and in vitro experiments involving exposure of tumor cells to bacterial supernatants. Beyond its intrinsic oncogenic effects, our integrative analysis of gut microbiota from patients with immunotherapy-treated GC revealed that S. anginosus is selectively enriched in non-responders and correlates with an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Furthermore, S. anginosus impairs CD8 + T-cell cytotoxic function, thereby attenuating the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade. Importantly, CD8 T-cell depletion experiments suggest that the protumor effects of S. anginosus are at least partly dependent on CD8 + T-cell related immune pathways, highlighting a key role of cytotoxic T-cell immunity in shaping its tumor-promoting activity. Together, these findings establish S. anginosus not only as a microbial driver of gastric tumorigenesis but also as a key regulator of antitumor immunity and immunotherapeutic resistance in GC. To elucidate the mechanism underlying S. anginosus -mediated immunosuppression, we focused on bacterial metabolites and identified KA as a key functional mediator. Colonization with S. anginosus increased KA in feces, bacterial supernatants, and intratumoral tissues in both mouse models and human GC samples. To elucidate downstream effectors of ITGA2, we performed mass spectrometry-based protein interaction analyses and identified CTSV as a key target. Functional rescue experiments confirmed that CTSV mediates ITGA2-dependent modulation of CD8 + T-cell activity. CTSV exhibits context-dependent roles in cancer, with its expression variably promoting or suppressing tumor progression across different cell types. 47 – 49 Elevated CTSV expression has been reported in multiple malignancies, including breast cancer, squamous cell carcinoma, and colorectal cancer. 50 – 52 However, its expression and regulatory functions within immune cells remain largely unexplored. Here, manipulating CTSV levels in CAR-engineered CD8 + T cells demonstrated that CTSV critically regulates their cytotoxic activity, highlighting a translationally relevant axis for enhancing adoptive T-cell therapies in cancer. Given that ITGA2 is a plasma membrane integrin whereas CTSV is predominantly localized to lysosomes, a direct spatial interaction is unlikely. Instead, our data support a signaling-mediated regulatory mechanism. Integrin signaling converges on the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, a key regulator of lysosomal function. In summary, our study delineates a causal axis linking S. anginosus colonization, metabolite-mediated suppression of cytotoxic CD8 + T cells, and gastric tumor progression. We demonstrate that S. anginosus -derived KA acts upstream to induce ITGA2 expression on CD8 + T cells, thereby engaging PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling and promoting CTSV-dependent T-cell dysfunction. Through this metabolite-integrin-mTOR-protease axis, cytotoxic CD8 + T-cell activity is attenuated, facilitating tumor immune escape. These findings highlight the importance of integrating microbial ecology with tumor immunology to better understand therapeutic resistance and develop microbiota-informed strategies for improving immunotherapy and CAR-T efficacy in GC. Targeting this metabolite-integrin-protease axis represents a promising strategy to restore antitumor immunity and enhance the efficacy of immunotherapy in GC. Several

Several limitations should also be acknowledged. Although our metabolomic analyses, GF mono-colonization experiments, and clinical correlation studies collectively support a contributory role of S. anginosus in driving KA accumulation, host-derived tryptophan metabolism may also participate in shaping intratumoral KA levels. In addition, definitive genetic evidence would require the construction of a KA synthesis-deficient S. anginosus mutant. However, stable genetic manipulation systems for clinical S. anginosus isolates remain technically challenging in our current experimental setting, particularly for precise editing of tryptophan metabolic pathways. Future studies using genetically engineered KA-deficient strains, isotope-tracing approaches, or bacterial metabolic flux analyses will therefore be important to further dissect the relative contribution of microbial versus host-derived KA within the tumor microenvironment. Moreover, while ITGA2 has known roles in regulating cell adhesion, migration, and tissue localization, these aspects were not investigated in the present study focused on the KA-ITGA2-AKT/mTOR axis in CD8 + T-cell dysfunction. Despite these limitations, our findings establish a mechanistic link between a tumor-associated bacterium, microbial metabolite-mediated immune regulation, and ICB resistance. This study highlights the importance of microbiome-derived metabolites as regulators of antitumor immunity and provides a potential therapeutic framework for overcoming immunotherapy resistance in GC.

Metabolic pathway activities are tremendously adaptive to adjust cellular and systemic homeostasis in response to external conditions, including nutrient availability. Specific tissues, such as the liver in vertebrates and the fat body in insects, serve as metabolic hubs that coordinate systemic homeostasis. This sets high requirements for signal integration, i.e., an ability to simultaneously read and combine information from multiple inputs to generate a coordinated metabolic output. Impaired integration of nutrient-sensing signals can lead to systemic pathophysiologies, such as metabolic syndrome and type II diabetes (Klein et al, 2022 ; Priest and Tontonoz, 2019 ). Protein kinase mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) is active when nutrients and energy are readily available, and it promotes the activity of anabolic pathways (Goul et al, 2023 ). mTORC1 activity is counteracted by the Forkhead box class O (FoxO) family of transcription factors, which activate catabolic genes (Xu et al, 2012 ) and inhibit mTORC1 activity, for example, by promoting the expression of its negative upstream regulator Sestrin (Lee et al, 2010 ). FoxO regulation integrates information from multiple sources: it is inhibited by insulin-like signaling through AKT-mediated phosphorylation (Brunet et al, 1999 ; Puig et al, 2003 ) and activated by several stress conditions, such as oxidative stress, heat, and genotoxic insults (Chen et al, 2010 ; Hopkins et al, 2025 ; Huang and Tindall, 2007 ; Rodriguez-Colman et al, 2024 ; Teleman et al, 2008 ). Spalt transcription factors are Zn-finger transcription factors with conserved regulatory roles in patterning and organogenesis (De Celis and Barrio, 2009 ). Mutations in two members of the human Sal-like (SALL) transcription factor family cause syndromes with impaired organogenesis, namely Townes-Brocks Syndrome (SALL1) and Okihiro Syndrome (SALL4) (Al-Baradie et al, 2002 ; Kohlhase et al, 1998 ). Their roles were originally discovered in Drosophila , where the two paralogs Spalt-major (Salm) and Spalt-related (Salr) regulate cell proliferation and survival downstream of Decapentaplegic (Dpp) signaling in the developing wing (De Celis et al, 1996 ; Sturtevant et al, 1997 ). Beyond development and organogenesis, however, the physiological roles of Spalt-like transcription factors are poorly understood. Here, we report an unexpected role of Drosophila Salr as a fasting-activated inhibitor of growth and lipid storage in fat body cells. Salr is deeply integrated into the core nutrient-sensing regulatory network, displaying striking and conserved similarities with FoxO in target gene binding profiles. Salr targets include components of the mTORC1 pathway, such as Sestrin and PRAS40 , and Salr is sufficient and necessary to restrict the growth-promoting activity of mTORC1 (Parmigiani et al, 2014 ; Wang et al, 2007 ). Salr and FoxO possess many similar functional properties, but they respond to distinct upstream cues. While FoxO is regulated by insulin-like signaling and displays rapid and transient activation upon fasting, Salr is activated through the integrated stress response (ISR) pathway during prolonged nutrient deprivation. Thus, our results imply that two converging pathways restrict growth, and they respond to fasting differentially depending on its duration and the upstream signaling cues involved.

When overexpressed in the fat body (CG-Gal4), Salr was sufficient to delay larval growth (Fig. 1A ) and pupariation (Fig. 1B ). In addition to systemic growth regulation, Salr overexpression in fat body clones (Tubulin [flipout] Gal4) strongly reduced cell size, demonstrating cell autonomous function (Figs. 1C and EV1A ). To test for possible functional conservation, we generated HepG2 hepatocellular carcinoma cells, moderately overexpressing Salr ortholog SALL1 (Fig. EV1C ). Salr and FoxO share common direct targets The nutrient responsiveness and target genes of Salr prompted us to explore its relationship with known regulators of nutrient-responsive transcription. One of the downstream effectors of ISR is the transcription factor Xrp1 (Brown et al, 2021 ), which we found to display chromatin binding close to the salr locus (Fig. EV6B ). Overexpression of Xrp1 in the fat body led to substantial fat body hypotrophy (Fig. 6B ), possibly due to its known effects in cell survival (Blanco et al, 2020 ). In line with the model of Xrp1 being an upstream activator of Salr, overexpression of Xrp1 led to markedly increased Salr expression (Fig. 6B ). We further tested the possibility of Xrp1 nutrient regulation and observed transiently elevated expression during fasting, which attenuated during prolonged fasting (Figs. 6C and EV6C ). Consistent with the hypothesis of Salr regulation by fasting-induced Xrp1 activation, knockdown of Xrp1 abolished the elevated Salr expression by prolonged fasting (Figs. 6D and EV6D ). Collectively, these data are consistent with a model that Salr and FoxO are activated by nutrient deprivation with differential kinetics and controlled by distinct upstream cues. Collectively, these data are consistent with a model that Salr and FoxO are activated by nutrient deprivation with differential kinetics and controlled by distinct upstream cues. Salr displays slow and sustained activation downstream of the ISR effector Xrp1, which is transiently activated during fasting, similar to FoxO.

This study provides evidence for two functionally converging stress response pathways that activate catabolic gene expression and restrict the activity of anabolic mTORC1 signaling. These pathways, controlled by Salr and FoxO transcription factors, respond to distinct upstream signals and are activated upon fasting with differential kinetics, FoxO displaying fast and transient activation and Salr being activated upon prolonged nutrient deprivation. Their functions appear mutually exclusive, as high expression of Salr during prolonged fasting promotes the attenuation of nuclear FoxO. ChIP-Seq data revealed high degree of overlap between the binding profiles, but future studies employing high-resolution binding site analysis are needed for more detailed insight for the molecular interplay between Salr and FoxO in the target promoters. The observed role for Salr as a regulator of metabolism and cell growth may appear surprising, regarding its well-established role in organogenesis (De Celis and Barrio, 2009 ). However, similar examples exist, including Cabut, a regulator of Dpp signaling in wing patterning, which also controls metabolic target genes as a downstream effector of intracellular sugar sensing and the circadian clock (Bartok et al, 2015 ; Bejarano et al, 2008 ). Our data show that Salr functions downstream of ISR and Xrp1, and it restricts mTORC1 activity in fat body cells. We observed that Xrp1 undergoes rapid and transient activation upon fasting and is necessary and sufficient to activate Salr, which displays a gradual and sustained activation pattern. mTORC1 activity in fat body cells. We observed that Xrp1 undergoes rapid and transient activation upon fasting and is necessary and sufficient to activate Salr, which displays a gradual and sustained activation pattern. Future work is needed to comprehensively address the role of fat body Xrp1 nutrient-responsive regulation of growth and metabolism, beyond its reported role as an upstream regulator of Salr. Previous work has shown that Xrp1 acts as a regulator of cell competition in developing Drosophila wing, being activated by proteotoxic stress and promoting the ‘loser’ status of cells destined to be eliminated (Baillon et al, 2018 ; Lee et al, 2018 ; Recasens-Alvarez et al, 2021 ). Interestingly, inhibiting mTORC1 activity can alleviate the elimination of cells with proteotoxic stress through stimulation of autophagy and allowing clearance of misfolded proteins (Recasens-Alvarez et al, 2021 ). Considering the observed role of Salr as a downstream effector of Xrp1 as well as a negative regulator of mTORC1 and activator of autophagy genes, it will be interesting to learn whether Salr contributes to proteotoxicity-induced cell competition in the wing imaginal disc. ChIPseq data derived from human hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells revealed pervasive overlap in genome-wide binding profiles of SALL1 and FOXO1, including the binding to promoters of mTORC1 upstream regulators, which suggests conservation of the observed functions in humans. FOXO1, including the binding to promoters of mTORC1 upstream regulators, which suggests conservation of the observed functions in humans. FOXO1 is a well-known tumor suppressor, and its expression is often reduced in HCC, which is associated with poor prognosis (Shi et al, 2018 ). Interestingly, SALL1 was also recently shown to function as a tumor suppressor in HCC and is sufficient to inhibit anchorage-dependent colony formation when highly overexpressed (Saito et al, 2025 ). Our findings in HepG2 cells confirmed these findings and showed that even moderately elevated expression of SALL1 is sufficient to potently inhibit the proliferation of HCC cells. Considering that mTORC1 is a major driver in HCC, being deregulated in about 50% of cases (Yu et al, 2019 ), it will be interesting to explore whether SALL1 and FOXO1 functionally converge to restrict mTORC1 activity in HCC, thereby suppressing tumorigenesis. In conclusion, our findings establish Salr, previously linked to organogenesis, as a core component of the regulatory network governing nutrient-responsive growth control. Through its role as an ISR-activated inhibitor of mTORC1 and FoxO, Salr function reveals previously unrecognized complexity in the interconnections between the core regulators of cellular homeostasis and their activation/attenuation dynamics during fasting. Future studies should address the role of Salr in modulating stress responses beyond nutrient deprivation.
